recent_posts.title: How Ramp used AI agents to patch 100 security vulnerabilities with no human involvement
recent_posts.summary: Ramp's security engineering team built a multi-agent pipeline that autonomously found, validated, and patched nearly 100 security vulnerabilities in their backend codebase in under a week, with no human involvement until PR review. The system used specialized detector agents for specific vulnerability classes (e.g., IDOR), adversarial manager agents to filter false positives (rejecting 40% of initial findings), a validator agent that wrote integration tests to confirm real issues, and a fixer agent that applied patches using test-driven development. The approach uncovered novel high-severity issues missed by penetration testing, bug bounties, and 10+ commercial scanning tools. The entire setup required only a four-hour hackathon and one week of work by a single engineer.

recent_posts.title: Why We Built Our Own Background Agent
recent_posts.summary: Ramp built Inspect, an internal background coding agent that writes and verifies code autonomously. Running in sandboxed VMs with full development environments, Inspect integrates with their entire tooling stack (Sentry, Datadog, GitHub, Slack) and supports multiple frontier models. The system achieves ~30% of all merged pull requests through fast session startup, unlimited concurrency, and multiplayer collaboration. The article provides a detailed technical specification for replicating their architecture, covering execution environments using Modal sandboxes, OpenCode agent integration, Cloudflare Durable Objects for state management, and client implementations including Slack bots, web interfaces, and Chrome extensions for visual React editing.

recent_posts.title: Meet Ramp Research: Our Agentic Data Analyst
recent_posts.summary: Ramp built an AI agent called Ramp Research that answers data questions directly in Slack, processing over 1,800 queries from 300 users since launch. The system combines metadata from dbt, Looker, and Snowflake with domain expertise documentation, using agentic reasoning to inspect data like a human analyst. This approach increased question volume by 10-20x compared to traditional data team workflows, enabling faster decision-making and reducing bottlenecks in data access.

recent_posts.title: Forward Deployed Engineering
recent_posts.summary: Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) has emerged as a critical role for B2B companies targeting enterprise customers. Originally created by Palantir, FDE involves engineers working directly with customers throughout their lifecycle to deliver customized solutions quickly. At Ramp, the FDE team grew from 2 to 16 engineers by focusing on customer outcomes, proper scoping, and generalizing solutions. Key principles include always questioning requirements, building scalable features, maintaining high velocity, and taking ownership of customer success. The role requires drive, engineering fundamentals, customer empathy, and strong communication skills rather than perfect technical performance.

recent_posts.title: How To Build Agents Users Can Trust
recent_posts.summary: Ramp built LLM-powered agents to automate expense approvals, achieving 65% automation rate. Key strategies include transparent reasoning with citations, allowing agents to express uncertainty, using categorical confidence levels instead of numerical scores, collaborative context improvement, and progressive autonomy from suggestions to full automation. The approach emphasizes building user trust through clear explanations, proper guardrails, and continuous evaluation with golden datasets.

recent_posts.title: How Ramp Fixes Merchant Matches with AI
recent_posts.summary: Ramp built an AI agent using LLMs, RAG, and embeddings to automatically fix incorrect merchant classifications for credit card transactions. The system resolves customer requests in under 10 seconds instead of hours, handling nearly 100% of requests compared to the previous 1.5-3% manual resolution rate. The agent uses multimodal context including transaction data, receipt images, and user memos, with careful guardrails to prevent hallucinations and inappropriate actions.

recent_posts.title: Turbo-Charging ML Development
recent_posts.summary: Ramp has developed a YAML-based configuration system called Turbo to speed up machine learning development and deployment. This system focuses on improving product velocity and reproducibility, essential for financial services. Turbo simplifies the creation of machine learning workflows, utilizing Python and Pydantic for abstraction. It enables developers to deploy ML models quickly and ensures consistent, reproducible results over time, enhancing overall productivity and efficiency.

recent_posts.title: Cost Efficient Snowflake CI
recent_posts.summary: Ramp tackles runaway Snowflake costs by applying operational rigor to data processes and implementing targeted cloning strategies. Employing ELT with Snowflake and dbt, they streamline Continuous Integration (CI) checks, reducing resource consumption and developer idle time. These optimizations involve using dbt artifacts and Snowflake’s zero-copy clones to avoid redundant model building, leading to significant cost savings and improved debugging capabilities.

recent_posts.title: Make Better Decisions by Embracing Uncertainty
recent_posts.summary: Ramp uses Thompson Sampling, a form of reinforcement learning, to improve the success rates of bank account linking. This algorithm dynamically balances exploration and exploitation, adapting to new data continuously. The implementation led to a significant increase in successful bank linkages and reduced the need for manual document uploads, enhancing the overall customer experience and efficiency.

recent_posts.title: Abstraction Engineering
recent_posts.summary: Ramp's initial product growth was driven by a set of opinionated best practices, but as complexity increased, more flexible solutions were needed. The company transitioned to a unified platform by building a generic workflows engine, improving flexibility and scalability. The solution involved using a graph-based data structure to enable complex workflows and integrating it with asynchronous task management backed by Postgres. The approach allowed for easier feature creation and significant performance improvements. The platform now supports various product functionalities and can handle over a million workflows daily.

top_posts.title: Rate limiting with Redis
top_posts.summary: Rate limiting is crucial in managing API usage and prevents overloading systems. Different rate limiting algorithms such as fixed-window, sliding window, leaky bucket, and GCRA offer various benefits and pitfalls. Ramp chose the GCRA algorithm for its efficiency and ease of implementation with Redis, tailoring it to handle multiple use cases. They continue to expand its application and monitor its performance.
